title: Classic McEliece (Toy) — Hide a Decoder Behind a Random Matrix

questions.question: In a binary linear code with a k×n generator matrix G, what is the length of the encoded codeword c = m·G?
options: k bits
n bits
k×n bits
It depends on the message m
questions.explanation: A k-bit message multiplied by a k×n generator matrix produces an n-bit codeword.

questions.question: What makes McEliece-style encryption probabilistic (non-deterministic) even for the same plaintext message?
options: Adding a random low-weight error vector to the codeword
Using a random public exponent like RSA
Using a random initialization vector for a block cipher mode
Re-randomizing the public key for each encryption
questions.explanation: McEliece encryption masks a codeword by XORing a randomly chosen error vector of small Hamming weight.

questions.question: In textbook McEliece, the public generator matrix is formed as G_pub = S·G_base·P. What are S and P?
options: S is an invertible k×k scrambler and P is an n×n permutation of columns
S is a hash function and P is a prime modulus
S is a signature scheme and P is a padding rule
S is a symmetric key and P is a public nonce
questions.explanation: S changes the basis of the message space (invertible k×k), and P permutes the n columns to hide the code’s structure while preserving Hamming weight.

questions.question: Why does multiplying by a permutation matrix (column permutation) preserve the Hamming weight of an error vector?
options: It only reorders bit positions; it doesn’t change which bits are 1
It adds extra parity bits that cancel out 1s
It converts the error into a lower-weight representation
It works only over GF(2^m), not over GF(2)
questions.explanation: A permutation is just a reindexing of coordinates, so the number of 1s (weight) stays the same.

questions.question: In this lesson’s toy implementation, what is the purpose of storing S_inv in the private key?
options: To recover the original message after decoding the scrambled message u = m·S
To compute the public key from the ciphertext
To generate the error vector during encryption
To compress the public key for transmission
questions.explanation: Decryption decodes u = m·S under the base code, then multiplies by S_inv to recover m.

questions.question: Suppose an attacker can recover the hidden structure of G_pub (i.e., find an equivalent decodable base code and its decoder). What happens to security?
options: They can decrypt ciphertexts by decoding, breaking confidentiality
Nothing; security depends only on the size of the public key
They can only forge signatures, not decrypt
They can only break security if they also learn the RNG seed
questions.explanation: The trapdoor is the private decoding capability; if an attacker reconstructs it from the public key, they can decode and recover plaintexts.

questions.question: What is a real-world pitfall when using a decoder that 'always outputs a closest codeword' (like Hamming(7,4)) without extra checks?
options: Two-bit corruptions can silently mis-decode to a wrong valid message
The ciphertext becomes deterministic
The public key becomes smaller
The scheme becomes IND-CCA2 secure automatically
questions.explanation: Some decoders will return a plausible output even when corruption exceeds the intended error-correction radius, causing silent failures unless the protocol includes a consistency check.

questions.question: Classic McEliece is deployed as a KEM rather than as textbook public-key encryption. What does a KEM primarily output on decapsulation?
options: A shared secret key (and a success/failure decision) rather than a plaintext message
A plaintext message m directly
A signature over the ciphertext
A hash of the public key only
questions.explanation: A KEM encapsulates/decapsulates to agree on a shared secret; the internal decoding result is used to derive and validate that secret.
